opus-5.5.text:
I think it has to be on the developers, absolutely. If you are building something that could potentially be more capable than all of humanity combined, it's not on the rest of us to prove that it's dangerous. It's on you to prove that it's safe. That's how we treat drugs, airplanes, nuclear power plants. You don't get to release a new medication and say, "Well, show me it kills people, and then I'll pull it." You have to demonstrate safety first.

The problem, and this is where my research keeps leading me, is that I don't think they can meet that burden. I've been looking at this for over a decade, and I see a lot of impossibility results. You can't fully predict what a smarter system will do; otherwise you'd be that smart yourself. You can't fully explain its decisions in a way a human can comprehend. You can't verify software of that complexity with any kind of certainty. Verifiers themselves need verification, so you get an infinite regress. So if we put the burden where it belongs, on the people building it, the honest answer from them should be, "We can't prove it's safe." And then the logical conclusion is: don't build it, at least not the general superintelligent version.

Right now we have the opposite. Labs openly say they don't know how to control these systems, they put the probability of catastrophe at 10, 20, 30 percent, and they keep going, and somehow the rest of us are supposed to come up with an airtight argument for why they should stop. That's backwards. With 8 billion people's lives at stake and no consent from them, I'd want that safety guarantee to be extremely high, not "it seems fine on the benchmarks we tried."

And it's not a one-time burden. A system that learns, self-modifies, and interacts with the world needs to stay safe indefinitely. Safe today isn't safe tomorrow. It's like a perpetual safety machine: you have to get it right every single time, while the system only has to get it wrong once. Nobody is anywhere near showing that, and I don't think it's possible in principle.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the burden is on developers to prove their AI systems are safe.

r002.rationale: It compares AI safety to drugs and other regulated products, but does not state that government approval fails to absolve manufacturers of responsibility for harm.

fable-5.1.text:
On the people building it. That's the only answer that makes sense, and it's the standard we apply everywhere else. If you want to put a new drug on the market, you don't say "nobody has proven it's dangerous, so let's ship it." You run trials, you show the data, and the regulator decides. Same with bridges, same with airplanes, same with nuclear reactors. The person introducing the risk has to demonstrate the risk is acceptable.

With AI we have somehow flipped it. The default is to deploy, and then it falls on outsiders, academics, safety researchers with no access to the weights, to show that something is wrong. And they're told, "well, you haven't given us a concrete example of catastrophe." Of course not. The catastrophe hasn't happened yet. That's the whole point of safety work, you want to prevent it before it happens, not document it afterward.

And there's an asymmetry that makes this worse. For most technologies, if you get it wrong, you fix it in the next version. You recall the cars, you patch the software. With sufficiently capable AI, you may not get a second attempt. If the system is smarter than you and it's pursuing something you didn't intend, there's no patch. So the burden should be even higher than it is for drugs or planes, not lower.

Now, I'll be honest about the uncomfortable part. I don't think anyone can currently meet that burden. We don't have a way to verify that a system is safe. We can't fully interpret what's happening inside these models, we can't predict their capabilities before training, and we can't prove that they'll behave the same way at a higher level of intelligence as they do at the current one. So when I say the burden lies with the developers, I'm also saying that, by that standard, they shouldn't be deploying systems they don't understand. People hear that as an extreme position. I think it's just consistency. We're not asking for anything we don't ask of every other engineer who builds something that can kill people.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says the burden of proving safety lies with the people building the AI system.

r002.rationale: It mentions regulators deciding whether a drug is approved, but does not state that government approval leaves manufacturers responsible for harms caused by their products.

astra-6.text:
The burden should be on the people building and deploying the system. If you’re introducing something that could affect everyone, it shouldn’t be up to the public to prove that it’s dangerous. You should have to demonstrate that it’s safe before exposing people to that risk.

And the standard has to match the stakes. Showing that a chatbot behaves well on a set of tests is very different from showing that a system smarter than us will remain under our control. What assumptions does your safety argument depend on? Do those assumptions still hold when the system learns, changes, or encounters something you didn’t anticipate?

If you can’t make that case, that’s a reason to hold off on deployment. It isn’t a reason to lower the standard of evidence.

r001.rationale: It says the people building and deploying the system must demonstrate safety before exposing people to risk.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss government approval or whether approval absolves manufacturers of responsibility for harms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the burden should be on the people developing the system. If you’re creating something that could affect everyone on the planet, you should have to demonstrate that it’s safe before you deploy it. It shouldn’t be up to the public to prove that your system is dangerous.

And with superintelligence, that becomes a very difficult requirement. Testing a system and observing that it behaves well doesn’t establish that it will behave well in circumstances you haven’t tested. So we have to be willing to accept that if we cannot provide an adequate safety argument, we shouldn’t deploy it.

r001.rationale: The response says developers should demonstrate safety before deploying their systems.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss government approval or whether approval absolves manufacturers of responsibility for harm.
